The Fed did not make a policy error yesterday by hiking rates. They ended a two-year policy mistake yesterday. Explained below.

1/3 The repost is correct. But the Fed adopted the PCE (orange) as its measure in 2000, not CPI (blue). Core PCE was 2.8% in Sept. 24 and was falling when the rate cuts began. It is now 3.3% and rising, as they started hiking. Viewed this way, hikes look more appropriate.

R to @biancoresearch: 2/3 The gap between core CPI/PCE is the largest since 1985, when the BLS switched to measuring housing inflation using Owner's Equivalent Rent (OER) and Rents of Primary Residence (RPR) OER plus RPR ~40% of core CPI ~17% of core PCE This is all about housing weightings.

R to @biancoresearch: 3/3 Which one should the Fed use? The one the Fed targets: PCE. And that measure suggests hiking was appropriate. --- CPI weights come primarily from the BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey and measure what households spend out of pocket. PCE weights come primarily from BEA business surveys and national-accounts data. They measure the broader set of goods and services consumed by households—including health care and other services paid for on their behalf by employers or the government. PCE also adjusts its weights more quickly as spending patterns change. That makes it broader and more responsive to substitution, which is why the Fed prefers it. --- Neither measure is “wrong.” CPI says housing-heavy, out-of-pocket inflation is cooling. OER has slowed to 3.06% and rent to 2.75%. PCE says broader inflation, especially away from housing, is strengthening. So the two measures are telling us different things: * Housing inflation is cooling. * Broader service inflation is not. For households, CPI may better capture the inflation they experience directly. But for the Fed, core PCE at 3.3% and rising is the more relevant signal, and it supports a hike.

I always look at Fed decision days this way. Day one is the overreaction. Day two is the reaction to day one. And day three is when you find out what the real next trends are going to be. This week makes it extra tricky because you have triple witching tomorrow and that is only going to accelerate what day three looks like. Buckle up. On the decision itself, the unanimous vote is what stands out to me. That is not a committee that is on the fence. That sets the table for future rate hikes and now the market has to think through a lot of things at once. We are transitioning from an easing cycle to a tightening cycle and that is a big deal. Not just for this week but for the fourth quarter. Oil I think has made a short-term high and could possibly have made the high for the rest of the year. If we get back down to the $96 area that is going to be the key place to watch. If it cannot hold $96 we go right back to the $84 area which was a magnet for several months. I do not love oil as a short here and I do not think it is a market I want to buy on a dip right now either. It is just a tricky trade. If oil does pull back toward $96 and lower, the bond market has likely made a low for the year. Gold starts to firm up. And the equity indexes, looking at what they did overnight, are already starting to think this through. Could we start to see all the indexes working together higher again? Even with the Fed starting to hike rates I think we can. It never matters what you think will happen going into these meetings. It is always about the reaction. The next 48 hours are key for establishing the primary trends. I would be very careful fading anything today. Whatever the trends were overnight I think they carry through the session. Do not stand in front of them. I am traveling and watching the markets without positions at the moment. What I am watching is the 30,400 level in the Nasdaq. If we start to clear that on a closing basis I will start looking at swing longs in NQ. And gold needs to clear $4,370 on a multiple daily closing basis before I start looking at it from the long side. Both of those are my triggers. Remember, patience is created through your preparation. Want this in your inbox every morning? It's free: http://anthonycrudele.com/newsletter Cheers, DELI

RT by @TheStalwart: Incredible episode from the gang. Going into the "listen-to-once-a-year-and-see-how-it-ages" folder. I have so many thoughts about this episode, and liberalism more broadly (https://clearlyintelligent.com/2026/01/29/a-defense-of-liberalism-past-present-and-future/) but I'll to compress a nuclear level take into a tweet. Liberalism is not meant to deliver meaning to man. Liberalism is meant to deliver a world in which finding meaning is more achievable, because Maslow-basic needs are more able to be met. In that piece, and overall, I argue that we've gotten away from that in the US in favor of corporatism and need to get back to Great Society liberalism if we want to actually move toward the world where the most people are the most able to find their own meaning. Another nugget here is that traditional forms of finding meaning (religion, childrearing, community) have fallen out of the cultural zeitgeist for many reasons. These are traditional ways to create your own meaning in life, and as people get further away from them, it means they are more on their own for creating their own meaning. When Joe has me on eventually, we can discuss all of this.
